newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Vietnamese editor seeks to reopen Cambodia paper.
newsitem.headline: Vietnamese editor seeks to reopen Cambodia paper.

text.p: An ethnic Vietnamese journalist deported last year for allegedly plotting to topple the Hanoi government is back in Cambodia and wants to reopen his newspaper.

Ly Chandara said on Tuesday he had written to the information ministry seeking permission to reopen his Tu Do, or "Freedom", newspaper by the end of January or early in February and wanted help and donations.
Information Ministry Secretary of State Khieu Kanharith said he had not seen any application from Ly Chandara, a Cambodian citizen, but saw no problem with the application.

However, Khmer Journalists Association co-president Pin Samkhon told Reuters that Khieu Kanharith and Information Minister Ieng Mouly had said "they want to make sure he has no problem with the Vietnamese Embassy".
Ly Chandara said his paper was closed in late 1995 by the information ministry, which cited intelligence reports that he was a top official in the anti-Hanoi organisation, Tu Do Vietnam.
He said he was arrested and deported to Vietnam with two other alleged anti-Hanoi activists on March 9 last year and was held in a prison in Ho Chi Minh City for almost eight months without trial.

"They accused me of being against the Vietnamese government. I am not anti-Hanoi but my newspaper wrote the facts about human rights violations (in Vietnam) and its name is Tu Do, like the movement Tu Do Vietnam (Free Vietnam)," he told Reuters.

Tu Do Vietnam is believed to be one of several anti-Hanoi groups led by former high-ranking members of the erstwhile U.S.-backed South Vietnam military that began operating in Cambodia after U.N.-run elections in 1993.
The Phnom Penh government began cracking down on them in 1995 and has since expelled or deported around 30 people, including U.S. citizens, for alleged involvement in these groups.
Ly Chandara said he was taken to Cambodia and released on October 10 after promising Vietnamese and Cambodian authorities not to plot against Vietnam or get involved in politics.

"I agreed to sign because I wanted to get out of prison ... I think they considered me a political prisoner," he said. One of the two men deported with him had also been released but the third, Ly Thara, was still in Vietnam, he added.
Pin Samkhon said he had advised Ly Chandara to keep a low profile after his return as he feared for his safety.
London-based Amnesty International and other human rights groups condemned the deportations at the time and said the three men faced possible persecution in Vietnam.
The deportations prompted a group of 13 ethnic Vietnamese to rush into the U.S. Embassy to seek asylum. They left after Cambodian officials promised that no action would be taken against them.
